historicalStatus: Interpretive scenes, not archaeological photographs or depictions of specific documented events.

Use case: historical-scene.
Asset type: one standalone horizontal website illustration, EXACT 16:9 aspect ratio, preferably 1536 x 864 pixels. Create a NEW image, not a website screenshot, no panels.
Art direction for a coherent three-image museum series: living ancient Chinese people with convincing anatomy, individual faces, real skin texture and weathered hands, natural gestures and tactile linen, timber, clay, bronze. Photorealistic historical cinema composed with the restraint and tonal depth of a fine-art painting, a quiet human moment rather than epic fantasy. Deep oxblood burgundy, warm umber, charcoal, worn ochre, subtle muted jade accents. Soft natural light illuminates people clearly against a dark warm background, atmospheric depth, restrained fine film grain, matte tactile surfaces. Dark wine red should anchor costumes or architecture, NOT a uniform red filter over faces.
Composition: a strong central axis with balanced groups on left and right; harmonious architectural symmetry but every person has a different natural pose, not mirrored copies. Medium-wide framing, people must be prominent and recognizable even in a small web card. Keep faces, hands and important actions within the central 80 percent of the frame with comfortable headroom. Both architecture and grounded human action are visible.
No lettering, no calligraphy, no text, no watermark, no collage, no border, no ornamental picture frame. No wax figures, no porcelain skin, no mannequin poses, no CGI, no 3D videogame render, no plastic or wet shiny surfaces, no glossy showroom, no neon, no magical glow, no fantasy armor, no aggressive HDR, no modern objects, no floating artifacts. This is an interpretive historical scene, not an exact depiction of a known archaeological event.
Scene: an ancestral offering ceremony inspired by Bronze Age Shang-Zhou central China, in a modest rammed-earth courtyard with heavy timber posts and no later imperial palace architecture.
Subject/action: at center a mature officiant in a plain deep-wine cross-collared ritual robe solemnly raises a small bronze wine vessel with both hands above a low wooden offering stand; a moderately sized sober bronze ding and ceramic grain bowls sit on it. Two attendants on each side bow or carry offerings, their different faces, hands and human gestures clearly visible. Natural tied hair and restrained cloth headwear, unbleached linen and muted burgundy clothes. The central human face remains visible, the vessel does not cover it.
Atmosphere: warm dawn skims the rammed earth, a slight wisp of woodsmoke, solemn stillness with subtle living motion in robes. The people, rather than an oversized pot, are the focal point.
Strictly peaceful offerings of grain and wine; no injury, no animal killing, no human sacrifice. Full composition 16:9.

Scene: a Western Han period workshop in the Liang region of central China, open timber bay and clay-plastered oxblood-brown walls, soft light through an open courtyard.
Subject/action: three ancient Chinese artisans actively work around a low broad wooden workbench. A seasoned craftsperson centered is carefully shaping a small clay funerary figurine with a wooden modeling tool, face and clay-dusted hands clearly readable; on the left another artisan burnishes a ceramic vessel; on the right a younger artisan polishes a modest bronze mirror with a cloth. Two or three finished clay figurines stand quietly on the workbench. The craft objects are humble work-in-progress, never oversized museum trophies.
Wear simple Han-era wrap tunics with belts, dark red/umber/unbleached hemp, tied hair or plain cloth caps, historically plausible sitting positions on low stools or mats. People interact naturally and concentrate on the craft, different expressions. No modern pottery machinery, no shiny gold.
Composition: centered workshop opening and centered workbench, left and right artisans balance it without identical poses. A real lived-in tactile workshop, poetry of hands and making. Full composition 16:9.

Scene: everyday civic life in a Ming-era walled town in central China inspired by Shangqiu, human-scale old brick gateway centered in depth, weathered timber shops on both sides and earthen street, neither fantasy imperial palace nor picturesque mountains.
Subject/action: ancient Chinese residents animated in a quiet morning market. In the foreground on the left a potter/vendor in a muted oxblood robe hands a modest pale ceramic bowl to a customer; on the right a craftsperson and a scholarly visitor examine an upright stone inscription under the shop eaves, the inscription is worn and abstract, no legible characters. Several middle-distance pedestrians cross naturally toward the centered gate. The foreground people are large enough to see real faces, hands and fabric, no tiny faceless crowd.
Clothing: modest Ming-era cross-collared robes, dark cloth caps or tied hair, no Qing shaved foreheads or queues. Soft morning sidelight touches worn plaster and fabrics; a faint damp sheen in part of the earth road can be subtle, not a mirror. Rich but restrained dark wine red, charcoal brick, warm natural skin and quiet ochre.
Composition: clear axial gateway, living activity on both sides with equal visual weight; lyrical natural light and human relationships, no rigid staged line of people. Full composition 16:9.
